title: Household air pollution and access to clean cooking, 2000–2023

sources.title: World Development Indicators: Access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking (% of population) (EG.CFT.ACCS.ZS)
sources.note: 原始提供者：WHO Global Household Energy Database。數值由 api.worldbank.org（WLD、SAS、SSF；lastupdated 2026-10-08）取得

sources.title: Goal 7: Ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all

facts.text: About 2.1 billion people still cook with solid fuels such as wood, charcoal, crop waste or dung, or with kerosene, on open fires or inefficient stoves.
Burning these fuels releases fine particles that go deep into the lungs and can enter the bloodstream.
In poorly ventilated homes, indoor smoke can hold fine particles at 100 times the acceptable level.
Household air pollution from cooking causes about 2.9 million premature deaths each year, including from heart disease, stroke and lung infections.
Women and children are most exposed because they spend the most time near the household fire.
Gathering fuel takes up a great deal of time for women and children and limits their education.
WHO counts electricity, gas and similar low-smoke fuels as clean for cooking.
In Sub-Saharan Africa, population growth has outpaced access, and 923 million people lacked clean cooking in 2022.
In 2021, 49 percent of rural people relied on polluting cooking fuels, compared with 14 percent of urban people.
SDG target 7.1 calls for universal access to modern energy services by 2030.
At the current pace, about 1.8 billion people will still rely on polluting cooking fuels in 2030.
South Asia’s share with clean cooking roughly doubled from 2010 (31.4%) to 2020 (62.6%).
The world share rose from 47.8% in 2000 (under half) to 74.5% in 2023 (about three-quarters).
